questions.text:
Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form
[latex]\forall x\left [P(x)\Rightarrow \exists yQ(x,y) \right ] [/latex]
where [latex]P[/latex] is a statement about integers, and [latex]Q[/latex] is a statement about pairs of integers. Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha's conjecture?
questions.solution:
Conjecture: for every x with P(x), some y makes Q(x, y) true.

- Option 1 talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.
- Option 2: Q holds for all x and y, so for any x any y works [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 3: one fixed y works for every x with P(x), so such a y exists for each x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] implies it.
- Option 4 again talks about only one x [latex]\text{---}[/latex] does not imply it.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.text:
Which one or more of the following CPU scheduling algorithms can potentially
cause starvation?
questions.solution:
Check whether a process can wait forever:
- FIFO: every process eventually reaches the front [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no starvation.
- Round Robin: each process gets a time slice every round [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no starvation.
- Priority scheduling: a low-priority process may wait forever if high-priority processes keep arriving.
- SJF: a long job may wait forever if short jobs keep arriving.

Answer: Priority Scheduling, Shortest Job First

questions.text:
Let [latex]f(x)=x^3+15x^2-33x-36 [/latex] be a real-valued function.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]f'(x)=3x^2+30x-33=3(x^2+10x-11)=3(x+11)(x-1)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] critical points [latex]x=-11[/latex] and [latex]x=1[/latex].

[latex]f''(x)=6x+30[/latex]:
- [latex]f''(-11)=-36 \lt 0[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] local maximum
- [latex]f''(1)=36 \gt 0[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] local minimum

Answer: f(x) has a local maximum and has a local minimum

questions.text:
Let [latex]f[/latex] and [latex]g[/latex] be functions of natural numbers given by [latex]f(n)=n[/latex] and [latex]g(n)=n^2[/latex].
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{g(n)}=\lim\frac{n}{n^2}=0[/latex], so f grows strictly slower than g.

- [latex]f\in O(g)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE
- [latex]f\in o(g)[/latex] (strictly smaller) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE
- [latex]f\in\Omega(g)[/latex] and [latex]f\in\Theta(g)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE

Answer: [latex]f\in O(g)[/latex] and [latex]f\in o(g)[/latex]

questions.text:
Let A be the adjacency matrix of the graph with vertices {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

Let [latex]\lambda _1,\lambda _2,\lambda _3,\lambda _4,\; and \; \lambda _5[/latex] be the five eigenvalues of A. Note that these eigenvalues need not be distinct.
The value of [latex]\lambda _1+\lambda _2+\lambda _3+ \lambda _4+ \lambda _5 =[/latex] _____
questions.solution:
Sum of eigenvalues = trace of A = sum of the diagonal entries.

A diagonal entry [latex]a_{ii}[/latex] is 1 only if vertex i has a self-loop. In the graph, vertices 3 and 4 have self-loops, so trace [latex]=1+1=2[/latex].

Answer: 2
